SUBJECT: Literature in English
LESSON TITLE: Revision
SUBTITLE (IF ANY): Literary Appreciation and Drama
PERIOD: 1st and 2nd
DURATION: 80 Minutes
LEARNING OBJECTIVES: Students will be able to
- List the components parts of the question;
- Discuss the Component parts sequentially;
- Correct errors made during the examination;
- Answer questions on each component better.
KEY VOCABULARY WORDS: genre, drama, prose, poetry, plot, setting,
Flashback, climax, conflict, picaresque, tragic flaw, prologue and epilogue
RESOURCES & MATERIALS: whiteboard, marker, flip-chart, the last term examination questions, the marking guide and students’ answer scripts.
BUILDING BACKGROUND/CONNECTION TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE:
Students are asked these questions:
- What is Literature?
- State three functions of Literature.
- List and define the three genres of Literature.
CONTENT: The examinations comprise questions on General Literary Knowledge, Drama and Prose.
Oral discussion of the different aspects of the question, questioning and marking guide will serve as the content of the lesson. N.B. [1] Literary appreciation [criticism) is a conscious attempt to see and understand all those things that are put together in a writing and find out whether they are good or bad when they all come together to make a short story, a novel, a poem or a play.
- Drama is a major work of literature that is either acted or read as a play.
- Prose as a major genre of literature is the art of story telling in a narrative style.
STRATEGIES AND ACTIVITIES: Review, Introduction, Conversational
Approach, Think-Pair-Share
LESSON SEQUENCE AND DELIVERY
ACTIVITY 1 (Review): The teacher guides the class to recap the last academic work through questions under the building background.
ACTIVITY 2 (Introduction): He introduces the lesson by writing the lesson title, learning objectives and key vocabulary words on the white-board and discusses them with the students.
ACTIVITY 3 (Conversational Approach): He guides the class to list sub-sets of the question paper, picks them in sequential order for a whole class discussion while the teacher provides the needed intellectual scaffolding [He offers support when and where necessary]
ACTIVITY 4 (Think-Pair-Share): Teacher asks Students to work in pair with a partner and take turns in quizzing each other on the questions and their answers. Let them swap partners and repeat the activity.
ACTIVITY 5 (Group Work): Teacher prompts students to work in small group of 5 or 6 and brainstorm on a subset of the questions and present their answer orally through a representative for a whole class discussion. The teacher clarifies, corrects or affirms students’ responses.
ASSESSMENT (EVALUATION): Teacher stops the class five to ten minutes early and asks students randomly to mention orally the most important things they have learned during the lesson.
WRAP-UP (CONCLUSION): Teacher concludes the lesson by guiding the students to sum up the major points discussed. He entertains questions from them to wrap-up the lesson.
ASSIGNMENT: Critically examine the themes and poetic devices used in the poem, “Black Woman” by Leopold Sedar Senghor.

WEEK 2
DATE:
CLASS: SS2
SUBJECT: LITERATURE IN ENGLISH
LESSON TITLE: STUDY AND ANALYSIS OF POETRY
SUBTITLE: ‘ONCE UPON A TIME’ BY GABRIEL OKARA.
PERIOD: 1&2
DURATION: 80 MINS.
OBJECTIVES: Students should be able to
- Explain the subject matter of the poem.
- Discuss the themes of the poem.
- Analyze the structure of the poem.
- Identify and explain poetic devices used.
KEY VOCABULARY WORDS: “laugh with their hearts, teeth, eyes, Shake hands without hearts, wear many faces,…”., muting, good riddance,
RESOURCES: The poem. Literature : An Introduction to Fiction, Poetry and Drama by X.L Kennedy and Dana Giola. Exam Reflection by S.O Faniyi. Simplified Literature Vol  II by F. Oyelekan . Flex, Pictorials, audio & video clips, Goggle, U-tube, etc
BUILDING BACKGROUND: Students will be encouraged to discuss how the study of poetry can be students will randomly discuss about the poet in answer to their last assignment.
CONTENT: The poem ONCE UPON A TIME is written in a simple, easy to understand form. It is presented in a narrative form. Structure like a mirror through which the poet views his past, compares it with the present and therein concluded to go back to his past because of the benefits he felt he had lost.
The poem is structured into 43lines, broken into 7 stanzas.
The first person narrative perspective is used. It is written in a Free verse form since the language does not follow a set rhyme pattern.
The mood is nostalgic filled with remembrance of a happier and simple past, sadness for the present status quo and a plea to achieve the euphoria of a peaceful past.
The poem recorded a discussion between a father and his son. The father used the storytelling indicator in narrating his observations and experiences. He opened up to the son on how he(the father),has been indoctrinated into the act of falsehood.
At the concluding part, the father registered his need for help soliciting the assistance of the son to revamp himself in order to rediscover the act of purity.
The poet’s use of a child like register contradicts the poem’s morals and views about growing up.
THEMES
- Loss of Innocence.: The poet mourn the loss of his innocence and the futility of imbibing a destructive culture.
- Change: The poet made known to the child that although change is natural not all are desirable. Based on the effects of change, one may find himself wishing for old status quo.
DEVICES
- Repetition: words like ‘face’, ‘laugh’, ‘smile’, ‘search’, ‘shake hands’, ‘show me’ and ‘once upon a time’ are repeated
- Enjambment.
- Alliteration: sounds like /f/ in ‘…home faces, office faces, street faces,…’stanza 3. /g/ in stanza 4’… goodbye, …good riddance, …glad…’
- Imagery: use of visual imagery like laughing with only the teeth, and how his laugh had become like a snake’s bare fangs!.
- Metaphor: ‘ while their ice- block-cold eyes…’ and others expressions like ‘… shake hands without my heart.’ are metaphorically used.
- Simile.  … ‘ show only my teeth like a snake’s bare fangs!’
STRATEGY: Recitation. Demonstration. Think pear share.
LESSON SEQUENCE:
STEP1. Students will recite the poetry trying as much as possible to create a n atmosphere of storytelling between a father and a son.
STEP 2. Students will identify and discuss the differences between the father’s observations, experiences and his present desire.
STEP 3. Students will analyze the themes they can identify. Students will be encouraged to think vast and deep on many meanings that can be aligned to the themes.
STEP 4. The structure of the poem will be studied.
The poem will be recited again in order to highlight the devices used and their purposes in the poem.
ASSESSMENT:
Analyze 3 reasons why the poet is willing to learn from his son.
Analyze the poets use of repetitions, Alliteration and Irony.
CONCLUSION: The poem is a sober, emotional poem with a strong moral message. It is serious throughout.
ASSIGNMENT: Read and study the poem ‘NEW TONGUE’ by Elizabeth Kamara.
HOD/VP’S COMMENT:
WEEK: 3
DATE:
CLASS: SS2
SUBJECT: Literature-in-English
LESSON TITLE: “New Tongue” by Elizabeth L. A. Kamara
SUBTITLE: Analysis of Content and Themes
PERIOD: 1st and 2nd
DURATION: 80 Minutes
LEARNING OBJECTIVES: By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:
i.      Identify and explain the subject matter and themes of the poem. Poem.
ii.      Identify and explain the poetic devices used by the poet in the poem.
iii.    Analyze the structure of the poem.
iv.    Answer questions on the poem by examiner.
KEY VOCABULARY WORDS: “New Tongue”, old tongue, borrowed tongue, a new generation, family, tradition, heritage, minds, culture, impregnable, future
RESOURCES AND MATERIALS: Cardboard or banner showing the lines of the poem.
REFERENCE BOOKS: Exam Reflection by S.O Faniyi. Simplified Literature Vol  II by F. Oyelekan . Flex, Pictorials, audio & video clips, Goggle, U-tube, etc.
BUILDING BACKGROUND/CONNECTION TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE: Teacher asks these probing questions from the Students:
- What are the themes of “Once Upon a Time” by Gabriel Okara?
- Differentiate the time in the past and the time in the present as seen in the poem.
- Mention some elements of poetry used by the poet in the poem.
CONTENT: “New Tongue” by Elizabeth L. A. Kamara is a forty-six-line poem that laments the neglect of African culture and tradition in the embrace of conveniently woke foreign values. The poem mourns the total detachment from tradition by a young generation of Africans as they adopt “borrowed” practices and confine the ashes of their own cultural practices “into the bottomless sea.”
THEMES OF New Tongue” by Elizabeth L. A. Kamara
- Theme of Cultural shift
The theme of cultural shift is the primary theme of Elizabeth Kamara’s “New Tongue.”
The theme is depicted by the new generation’s adoption of the “new tongue and their embrace of a different culture, which results in a complete transformation in the way they think, speak and interact. The poet captures this using “impregnable chains” to show the strong and unbreakable attachment to new culture which has profound impact on their identities. The title, “New Tongue” indicates linguistic shift, adoption of new language by this new generation. They adopt now dances and dispose old songs as disregarded dreams, symbolic of a generational change in social and cultural changes. There is also a break in ties within family and friendship. There is shift from collectivism to individualism. In line 4, the poet describes that “Their eyes revel in the wonder of the new.” This mean that they are enthusiastic about the adopted culture, they even celebrate by “Glorying in their newness of a borrowed tongue and culture.”
2. Theme of Generational Conflict
The poem talks about the strained relationship between generations. No room for elders in the minds of the new generation, whose ears are metaphorically blocked to the “old tongue” and traditional ways. Of doing things.
The poem draws evident line between the younger generation who speak a “new tongue” and dance to “new dances” with no respect for tradition, and older generation, who are symbolized by the “ashes strewn into the bottomless sea” and “disregarded dreams.” The new generation rejects old ways, are indifferent to the wisdom of elders and deliberate distancing from traditional values and practices.
There is rejection of familial ties and disdain for friendship by the younger generation highlights The generational divide even more. This obviously causes a rupture in the intergenerational relationships that were once considered fundamental in Africa (lines 8-7, 14-16, and 38-41)
3. Theme of Loss
One obvious loss in the poem is the loss of cultural heritage. The old songs and ties of family and friendship are described as “disregarded dreams” and “loosened, broken, burnt.” This signifies a deliberate departure from established cultural norms and values. Expressions like “ashes strewn into the sea” and “hang the last lock on their culture” emphasize the finality and irreversibility of this loss.
POETIC DEVICES
Elizabeth Kamara employs various poetic devices to convey cogent messages, emotions and ideas to the readers. Here are some poetic devices used in the poem:
- Imagery
The use of auditory imagery - “Their ears blocked to the old tongue”  Tactile imagery - “or like bathing…
Sensory imagery of food
(as fishes swim by); music (song, dance); clothing (Like the insides of clothes, Tugging of skirts).
Visual imagery - “Their eyes revel in the wonder of the new,”” And swirling debris in the air; The gusts of wind falling trees” “… parted the red sea long ago.
ii. Metaphor
Language is compared to a” new tongue” to emphasize its transformative power. Another metaphor is “…impregnable chains” to show how the new generation is bound to the new culture. The word, “old”, is another metaphor to compare everything related to old generation and ways of doing things, it also stands for elderly ones. Another one is “… bound hearts and minds” for the entirety of humanity in slavery to new culture.
iii. Symbolism
The use of “new tongue” or “old tongue” represents cultural identity, language and belonging.
Songs, clothes, dreams, family, friendships are representations of cultural heritage.
iv. Alliteration
The repetition of initial consonant sounds in the poem shows the level of musicality. This can be seen in the following lines l2 and l6 - dance new; disregarded dreams  l8 - family and friendship l9 - broken sent burnt
l44 - last lock
v. Enjambment (run on lines)
Sentences or phrases continue into the next line without punctuation. This creates a sense of flow, reflecting the personae’s stream-of-consciousness
vi. Personification
The poet personified “new tongue” and “old tongue” these are personification of language.
vii. Repetition
There are some words and phrases that are repeated for emphasis: new (4 times from l1-4 and 14) and newness I  line 30); old (2 times); himself (3 times), borrowed (2 times); culture (2 times).
viii. Alliteration
There is  Biblical allusion in the poem - “Their borrowed minds parted the read sea long ago,” this is a reference to the Israelites’ journey from Egypt to Cannan Land going through the red sea after it was parted, they actually borrowed actually some things from the
Egyptians before they left and that event occurred a time in the past” … long ago.”
ix. Simile
In line 23, the poet compares how the minds of the younger generation have turned away totally to the culture, tradition and heritage of the elders “…like the insides of clothes” A strange coldness descending. like snow covered mountain/Or like bathing at the back of the house This shows how the borrowed tongue and culture have made the younger generation to be unresponsive to their old native culture and language.
STRATEGY AND ACTIVITIES: Review, Introduction, Conversational Approach, Recitation, Demonstration, Think-Pair Share.
LESSON SEQUENCE:
ACTIVITY 1: The teacher inspires the students to recapitulate the content of the previous lesson.  ACTIVITY 2: Teacher writes and shares with the students the lesson topic, learning objectives and key vocabulary words.
ACTIVITY 3: Teacher guides the students to recite the poem and interpret the poem line by line and  stanza by stanza.
ACTIVITY 4: Students, in small groups brainstorm on the subject matter of the poem.
ACTIVITY 5: Students, in pairs, share thoughts on the themes of the poem. The representatives of the pairs share their discussion. The teacher guides against errors.
ACTIVITY 6: The teacher guides the students to recite the poem again in order to highlight the devices used and their significance in the poem. They also discuss the structure of the poem.
ASSESSMENT: Teacher asks these questions from the students:
1) Discuss 3 themes of the poem.
2) Analyzethe poet’s use of repetition, alliteration and simile.
WRAP UP/CONCLUSION: Teacher reviews the lesson content with the students and asks if the objectives of the lesson is achieved. The teacher emphasizes the fact that poet is emotionally troubled about how the younger generation quickly wanders away with the new culture in all forms and forgetting their previous rich culture, norms and values.
